opus-5.5.text:
I think the hardest part isn't the geometry. People often assume Real2Sim is mainly a reconstruction problem: scan the scene, get a nice mesh or a Gaussian splat, and you're done. Visually that has gotten remarkably good in the last few years. You can capture a kitchen with a phone and render it almost photorealistically.

The real difficulty is physics, the things you can't see. When you look at a cup on a table, the camera tells you its shape and color. It doesn't tell you the mass distribution, the friction coefficient between the cup and the table, how compliant the material is, whether there's liquid inside, or how a drawer's hinge resists when you pull it. For a robot those invisible properties matter more than what the object looks like. A grasp that works in simulation can fail completely in the real world because the friction is off by a factor of two.

So there's an asymmetry. Appearance is observable from passive capture, but dynamics usually have to be inferred through interaction. You have to push things, lift them, open them, and then solve an inverse problem to estimate the parameters. That's slow, it doesn't scale the way scanning does, and the problem is often ill-posed, because many different parameter combinations can explain the same short interaction.

The second hard part is articulation and structure. A scanned mesh is just a surface. It doesn't know the cabinet door is a separate rigid body connected by a revolute joint, or that the cable is deformable. Turning a pretty reconstruction into something simulatable means segmenting parts, inferring joints and their limits, and assigning the right physical model to each component. That's semantic understanding as much as reconstruction.

The third is fidelity versus usefulness. You never get a perfect digital twin, so the question becomes what level of accuracy actually matters for the task. Sometimes a rough approximation plus domain randomization transfers better than a carefully tuned but slightly wrong model. Knowing where to spend fidelity is almost a research question in itself.

If I had to put it in one sentence: making it look real is mostly solved. Making it behave real, at scale and without a person carefully tuning every object, is the frontier.

r001.rationale: It says visual reconstruction is largely solved and identifies making the scene behave realistically as the frontier.

r002.rationale: It explains that simulation needs object properties such as mass, friction, compliance, and joints, beyond appearance.

r003.rationale: It mentions a drawer hinge resisting when pulled, but does not state that the force to open a refrigerator door varies with its opening angle.

r004.rationale: It distinguishes rigid and deformable objects but does not compare the maturity of their simulation.

fable-5.1.text:
The hardest part, honestly, isn't the geometry. People assume Real2Sim is about getting the shapes right, scanning a kitchen or a warehouse and dropping it into a physics engine. That part has gotten much easier. You can do a reasonable reconstruction from a phone video now.

What's hard is everything you can't see. Friction coefficients, the compliance of a cable, how a plastic bottle deforms when you grip it too hard, the way a door hinge sticks a little before it swings. None of that shows up in a point cloud. And those are exactly the things a robot policy ends up depending on. You train in a world where the mug slides perfectly on a table, and then in the real lab the mug catches on a crumb and the whole grasp fails.

So the real problem is identifying the parameters that matter for the task, and then estimating them from limited interaction. You can't measure everything, so you have to be selective. I think of it as asking: what would break the policy if it were wrong? Then you put your effort there and let the rest be approximate.

The second thing, and this one gets underestimated, is the long tail. A single scene is tractable. A hundred scenes with the variation you'd actually encounter in deployment, different lighting, clutter, objects that have been moved since you scanned, that's where the pipeline either scales or it doesn't. If every scene needs a human to go in and tune contact parameters by hand, you don't really have Real2Sim, you have a very expensive demo.

So I'd say: the invisible physics, and making the whole thing automatic enough that you can do it a thousand times instead of once.

r001.rationale: It says geometry is not the hard part and identifies invisible physics, such as friction and compliance, as the main challenge.

r002.rationale: It explains that simulated assets need task-relevant physical properties, including friction, compliance, and deformation.

r003.rationale: It gives a door hinge as an example but does not say that the force to open a refrigerator door varies with its opening angle.

r004.rationale: It does not compare the maturity of rigid-body and deformable-body simulation.

astra-6.text:
I think the hardest part is capturing the things you can’t directly see. You can reconstruct the geometry of a scene and make it look convincing, but that doesn’t tell you how it behaves. How much friction is there between two surfaces? How does an object deform when you grip it? Those properties matter enormously when a robot starts interacting with the world.

And the observations can be ambiguous. If an object moves less than you expected when you push it, is that because it’s heavier, because the friction is higher, or because your estimate of the applied force is wrong? Several different simulations might explain the same observation, yet predict very different outcomes for the next action.

So the challenge is deciding what you need to measure and how accurately you need to model it for the task. I’d want a simulation that reproduces the interactions we care about, with an honest representation of uncertainty. A visually perfect reconstruction alone doesn’t give you that.

r001.rationale: The response says the hardest part is capturing how things behave and that a visually convincing reconstruction alone is insufficient.

r002.rationale: It discusses friction and deformation as important physical properties, but does not state that assets mapped into simulation must encode those properties.

r003.rationale: It does not mention refrigerator doors or opening-angle-dependent force.

r004.rationale: It does not compare the maturity of rigid-body and deformable-body simulation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the hardest part is capturing the properties you can’t directly see. You can reconstruct the geometry of a scene, but that doesn’t tell you how much friction a surface has, how heavy an object is, or how it deforms when you touch it. Those properties determine what happens when a robot interacts with the world.

And different physical parameters can produce very similar observations. So the challenge is figuring out what you need to measure, and which interactions will reveal it. Ultimately, a useful simulation has to reproduce the consequences of the robot’s actions, not just the appearance of the scene.

r001.rationale: It identifies capturing physical properties and reproducing the consequences of robot actions, rather than scene appearance, as the central challenge.

r002.rationale: It names physical properties of surfaces and objects, but does not state that assets mapped into simulation must encode those properties.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss refrigerator doors or opening force varying with door angle.

r004.rationale: It does not compare the maturity of rigid-body and deformable-body simulation.
